stances.claim: The proposal to abolish the JBC and return to the President + Commission on Appointments system is misguided: under the old system, no SC appointee was ever rejected by the CA despite some proving unworthy, and the old hearings were demeaned by crude questions and demands for personal favors.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-failure rebuttal: using the CA system's own zero-rejection record as proof of its inadequacy

stances.claim: The Constitution should be amended to have the Supreme Court appoint three JBC members (retired justices, integrated bar, law professors) while the President retains the private-sector representative and each chamber of Congress gets one member — creating a 4-4 balance between judicial and political branches.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-reform proposal: rebalancing JBC composition to reduce political pressure while preserving democratic representation
stances.confidence: recommended as a future constitutional amendment

stances.claim: Post-Corona, the JBC must comb candidates' SALNs and ITRs and grill them on their familiarity with all eight chief justice duties, vision-mission for reform, and plans to speed up the delivery of quality justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: impeachment-lesson-as-reform-standard: using the Corona SALN scandal as the operational template for JBC vetting

notable_anecdotes: CJ Concepcion's lament that the old CA confirmation hearings 'demeaned the appointees not only with crude and impertinent questions but also with demands for personal favors' — deployed as the historical justification for the JBC system, directly contrasting its dignity-preserving design with the political circus it replaced.

Judge Sandra Oxner's study showing the JBC's council model has been adopted in 20+ countries, with France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain having councils that actually appoint (not just nominate) judges — used as international validation for strengthening rather than abolishing the JBC.

The unnamed justice who was snubbed at his retirement dinner after being 'held liable for grave misconduct for leaking a confidential internal document and fined P500,000' — used in prior context as a cautionary example of the post-impeachment scrutiny now being applied to the chief justice selection process.

one_paragraph_summary: Writing as daily live-media-coverage JBC interviews begin July 24, 2012 for the chief justice vacancy, Panganiban identifies the JBC's central challenge: to prove in its 25-year history that the council system works -- interviewing candidates assiduously but not rudely, scrutinizing thoroughly but not brusquely -- while critics push to abolish it and return to President + Commission on Appointments appointments. He rebuts the abolition proposal by noting that under the old CA system, no SC appointee was ever rejected despite some proving unworthy, and that CJ Concepcion specifically designed the JBC to replace confirmation hearings that 'demeaned appointees with crude questions and demands for personal favors.' He cites Judge Oxner's study showing the JBC model has been adopted in 20+ countries (with France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain having councils that actually appoint judges) as proof of a growing international depoliticization trend. He proposes a future constitutional amendment: the SC should appoint three JBC members (retired justices, integrated bar, law professors) while the President retains the private-sector representative and each congressional chamber gets one member, creating a 4-4 judicial/political balance. Post-Corona, he urges the JBC to comb candidates' SALNs and ITRs and grill them on familiarity with all eight chief justice duties, vision-mission for reform, and plans to speed up the delivery of quality justice.
